newsitem.title: THAILAND: Views mixed on when Thailand may end capital controls.
newsitem.headline: Views mixed on when Thailand may end capital controls.

text.p: Views remain mixed about when Thailand will lift the two-tiered system designed to defend its battered currency.

Some traders and analysts polled on Friday said ending the controls could come within a week as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) may be eager to remove any such capital controls as soon as possible.
But others predicted the IMF may prefer to wait, possibly for some months, until it becomes clear that investor confidence has returned to the Thai currency.

"If the IMF had not come in, the two-tier system might have lasted quite a long time. But I think the IMF package changed that possibility," said George Morgan, country chief executive of ABN Amro Hoare Govett.
He added that Thailand was likely to drop the two-tier market soon after existing forward contracts mature within a few weeks.

The two-tier currency market -- one onshore and one offshore -- was imposed in May to cut off baht supplies from local sources to offshore speculators attacking the currency, forcing them to scramble for baht to cover short positions.
Speculators at that time built up short baht positions in the forward market, which mature in the next few days.
Thailand has repeatedly said that it would lift the controls as they were temporary measures, but neither the central bank or the IMF has hinted at any specific timing.
A currency trader at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi in Bangkok said that the control could be lifted after August 21, when the IMF is due to formally adopt a rescue package for Thailand.
The IMF and Asian nations came up with a $16 billion loan package in exchange for Thailand's pledge to take austerity steps to pull its economy out of its worst slump in decades.
However, other analysts warned that it was premature for Thailand to lift the controls because the Thai economy and baht remain far from stable.
They said Thailand and the IMF need at least one or two months to assess the impact of harsh economic steps on the economy such as the increase in the value-added tax on Saturday.

"You cannot rule out the possibility of yet another tumble in the baht (if) Thailand removes its capital controls," said a major Japanese bank official in Bangkok. "I don't think Thailand would dare to take the risk any time soon."
The baht has plunged more than 20 percent against the dollar since July 2 when Bangkok replaced a 13-year system of pegging its unit to a basket of currencies with a managed float.

ABN's Morgan said that the baht would be more exposed to speculative attacks if Thailand dropped the two-tier market, but the market would be more liquid as the controls choke off liquidity for everyone, not just speculators.
"It's two sides of the same coin," Morgan said.
An analyst at a Thai Military Bank affiliate said that the Bank of Thailand still needed to learn how to manage the floating currency system and it must first negotiate with the IMF.

"It depends on conditions. (The IMF) must be assured that the baht will stabilise and there will be no further speculative attacks... In about three to six months, there should be the time for the central bank to consider removing the two-tier system." -- Bangkok newsroom (662)-6520642 -- email:bangkok.newsroom@reuters.com
